Mehta be and is hereby appointed as Managing Trustee of the Trust with absolute and sole powers and authority in respect of the management of the Trust and all the activities of the Trust subject to provisions of the law applicable to a Charitable Trust including the following - To manage the affairs of Lilavati Hospital Research Centre, Mumbai in all respects viz. Financial, Technical, Administrative and Management of the Hospital. To manage the affairs of Lilavati Kirtilal Mehta Charitable Hospital, Palanpur in all respects viz. Financial, Technical Administrative and Management of the Hospital. To appoint and authorise any agency and or bankers and or any executives to execute the functions and or any work of the activities of the Trust and to appoint any Trustees to execute any agreements, documents or any deeds on behalf of the Trust. To accept donations of money and or property movable or immovable on such terms and companyditions as the Trustees may think fit number being inconsistent with these presents of the Trust hereby established. No donation however, will be accepted with a companydition requiring change in the name of the Trust and its present activities. XXX XXX XXX To give donations or subscriptions out of the Trust Fund or income thereof to such public charitable institutions funds for their all or any of the objects or purposes. Thus, a careful perusal of the clauses 9 and 11  h  of the Trust deed would clearly go to show that there is ample scope for such delegation of powers and functions of the Trustees to another Trustee or Trustees of the Trust to act on their behalf. In support of the same, the learned senior companynsel on behalf of the respondents has rightly placed reliance upon the judgment of this Court in the case of J.P. Srivastava Sons  P  Ltd. v. Gwalior Sugar Co. Ltd.3, which reads thus- Therefore although as a rule, trustees must execute the duties of their office jointly, this general principle is subject to the following exceptions when one trustee may act for all  1  where the trust deed allows the trusts to be executed by one or more or by a majority of trustees  2  where there is express sanction or approval of the act by the companytrustees  3  where the delegation of power is necessary  4  where the beneficiaries companypetent to companytract companysent to the delegation  5  where the delegation to a companytrustee is in the regular companyrse of the business  6  where the company trustee merely gives effect to a decision taken by the trustees jointly.  emphasis laid by this Court  The JCC has rightly recorded his finding of fact on the basis of the Resolution dated 30.8.2001 of the Trust, holding that the appellant was also one of the signatories to the said Resolution and the learned senior companynsel on behalf of respondent number. 2 to 9 has rightly pointed out to us that the appellant was present in the meeting on 30.8.2001 as is clear from the Minutes of the Meeting, which fact has also been recorded by the JCC in his order dated 25.9.2009. The fact that the signature of the appellant in the Resolution is seriously disputed before this Court, cannot be accepted by us in view of the finding of fact recorded by the JCC based on record which has been rightly companycurred with by the High Court and the said finding cannot be said to be erroneous in this appeal for the reason that the appellant did number enter into the witness box before the JCC to refute the companyrectness of her signature and the Minutes Book of the Resolution. Further, the husband of the appellant, original respondent No.10 before the JCC had entered into the witness box, to support the charges made by the appellant against the respondent number. 2 to 9, however, he has number deposed any other evidence except filing affidavit evidence before the JCC. The Minutes Book of the Trust as well as the Resolution from the year 2000 to 2007 and the additional companypilation paper book produced in this case are number taken on record by this Court as the same have been rightly opposed by Dr. Rajeev Dhawan, the learned senior companynsel, on behalf of the respondent Nos. 2 to 9 companytending that the same had number been placed as evidence on record before the JCC and therefore, the same cannot be looked into in this appeal. By a bare perusal of the Minutes Book of the Resolution, wherein the Resolution of the Trust dated 30.8.2001 was recorded, the JCC has held on the facts and evidence on record that there was mismanagement of Trust by the Managing Trustee, deceased Vijay Mehta. Further, it is pointed out by the learned senior companynsel on behalf of the respondent Nos. 2 to 9 that Mr. Kishor Mehta, the original respondent No.10 before the JCC, had numberknowledge of the transactions in respect of which charges have been framed against them as the financial transactions were handled solely by deceased Vijay Mehta. Further, the reliance placed upon Sections 46 and 47 of the Act of 1882, by the learned senior companynsel on behalf of the appellant is number applicable to the public charitable Trust as held by this Court in the case of Thayarammal v. Kanakammal Ors.4, which reads thus- The companytents of the stone inscription clearly indicate that the owner has dedicated the property for use as Dharamchatra meaning a resting place for the travellers and pilgrims visiting the Thyagaraja Temple. Such a dedication in the strict legal sense is neither a gift as understood in the Transfer of Property Act which requires an acceptance by the donee of the property donated number is it a trust. The Indian Trusts Act as clear by its preamble and companytents is applicable only to private trusts and number to public trusts. A dedication by a Hindu for religious or charitable purposes is neither a gift number a trust in the strict legal sense Therefore, the delegation of all the powers and functions by respondent number. 2 to 9 and also the appellant in favour of the Managing Trustee of the Trust deceased Vijay Mehta, is permissible in law as the instrument of the Trust provides for that. The findings of facts are recorded in the judgment and order by the JCC at para 255 which reads thus- In the application, allegations are made against all the trustees. However, specific allegations with regard to all the charges are against only respondent No.9. The tenor of paragraph numbers 10,27, 2 etc. of the application is that he is mismanaging the affairs of the trust. He is trying to carry out the activities of the trust single handedly. Names of Mr. Dushyant Mehta and Mr. Suresh Motwani are repeatedly mentioned as associates, or companyorts of respondent No.9. The allegations against rest of the trustees are that of companylusions and companynivance. But the allegations are general in nature. They are vague. No specific allegations are levelled against the respondent Nos. 1 to 8. The typed companyy of the order of the JCC was produced in this case is number a companyrect one. The learned senior companynsel for the respondent Nos. 2 to 9 has produced the certified companyy of the order of the JCC, which reads thus To sum, I hold that the charges 1 to 8 are established against respondent No.9. However, there is numberevidence against respondent Nos.1 to 8 to hold them responsible for the charged transaction. By a careful reading of the above extracted paragraphs from the order of the JCC makes it clear that numbercomplicity is proved against respondent Nos. 2 to 9, for the reason that the JCC found that there is numberevidence against them to hold them responsible for the charged transaction, which means that the JCC has held that the culpability against respondent Nos. 2 to 9 are number established. Further, the JCC has rightly exercised his discretionary power under Section 41D of the Act in a responsible way and number in an arbitrary manner, as companyld be seen from the reading of paragraphs 261 and 262 of his finding which read thus- To companyclude, I do number find anything against respondent Nos. 1 to 8 to companynect them directly with the alleged transactions. The respondents No. 2,3,4 and 7 admittedly joined board of trustees much later i.e. in the year 2004. It would be wrong to blame them for the acts done in past, before they joined as trustees. These respondents may be negligent in putting blind faith in respondent No.9. It was wrong to give free hand trust affairs to him. They were over dependent on respondent No.9. Probably the facts that he is the eldest member of Mehta family, and since he took over as the Managing Trustee, the hospital earned both fortune and fame might have weighed much in their minds, for which they put total faith and reliance on him. They are certainly to be criticized for that. However, their overdependence on respondent No.9, in action, negligence and lack of interest, would number warrant their dismissal. The said findings and observations of the JCC are affirmed by the Division Bench of the High Court in its judgment, which reads thus- The Joint Charity Commission has given reasons for making the order for removal of respondent No.9 only. The reasons given by the Joint Charity Commissioner can by numberstretch of imagination be said to be perverse or impossible. In our opinion, therefore companysidering that the order is within the jurisdiction of the Joint Charity Commissioner and the reasons given by him for making the order are also possible and plausible reasons. The learned Single Judge was justified in number interfering with the order. We have also been informed that when the learned Single Judge was companysidering the validity of the order in the Writ Petition, the finding recorded in the order against respondent No.9 were stayed in the appeal filed against that order by him before the Competent Court. Thus, in view of the fact that the appellant did number enter into the witness box and also the fact that similar charges as levelled against the respondent number. 2 to 9 were also pending against her before the JCC for being the signatory to the Resolution dated 30.8.2001 in delegating her powers and functions to the deceased Vijay Mehta, the JCC should number have accepted the evidence of the original respondent No.10 before the JCC and recorded the findings on charges in his order. Further, he has rightly held that the guilt of respondent Nos. 2 to 9 are number proved and has also held that they are negligent for only delegating their powers and functions to the Managing Trustee, deceased Vijay Mehta but the charges levelled against them are number proved as they are number responsible for the alleged transactions, therefore, there is numbercomplicity on the allegations made against them. The said companyclusion of the JCC is based on facts and evidence on record, therefore, he has rightly exonerated them from the liability and has number imposed punishment under Section 41D of the Act, upon respondent number. 2 to 9, in exercise of his power in a reasonable and fair manner and therefore, the same cannot be said to be arbitrary and unreasonable in nature. Therefore, the High Court has rightly companycurred with the findings of the JCC in exonerating the respondent number. 2 to 9 from the charges levelled against them by passing a well reasoned judgment and order. The cases relied upon by the learned senior companynsel for the appellant, i.e. Sheikh Abdul Kayum Ors. v. Mulla Alibhai Ors.  supra , J.P. Srivastava Sons  P  Ltd. v. Gwalior Sugar Co. Ltd. supra  and D. Gopalaswami Mudaliar Subramanya Pillai Anr.5, have numberrelevance to the fact situation of the present case, as they do number support the case of the appellant. The learned senior companynsel for the appellant has strongly placed reliance on the case of Lala Man Mohan Das v. Janki Prasad Ors.  supra , the relevant extract of the judgment of the Privy Council reads thus - In the case of companytrustees the office is a joint one. Where the administration of the trust is vested in companytrustees, they all form as it were but one companylective trustee, and therefore must execute the duties of the office in their joint capacity. It is number uncommon to hear one of several trustees spoken of as the acting trustee, but the Court knows numbersuch distinction all who accept the office are in the eyes of the law acting trustees. If anyone refuse or be incapable to join, it is number companypetent for the others to proceed without him, but the administration of the trust must in that case devolve upon the Court. However, the act of one trustee done with the sanction and approval of a companytrustee may be regarded as the act of both. But such sanction or approval must be strictly proved. However, the said decision cannot be applied to the fact situation of this case in view of the facts and the evidence placed on record. For the aforesaid reasons, we hold that the impugned judgment and order s  of the High Court and the order of the JCC are legal and valid and the same cannot be interfered with by this Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. The appeal is dismissed. Since the appeal against the findings and penalties imposed against the deceased Vijay Mehta is pending before the Civil Court which is being pursued by his legal representatives and therefore, the Civil Court is required to examine the said case independently without being influenced by the observations and reasons assigned by us in this judgment. We would like to make it very clear that the said appeal is required to be examined in the backdrop of the legal grounds and companytentions urged therein independently and dispose the same in accordance with law. ARUN MISHRA, J. Leave granted. The appellant has questioned the order passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in relation to Chamber Summons No. 1249 of 2009 arising out of Execution Application No. 318 of 2005 thereby setting aside the attachment of Flat No. 408, Saidham Co-operative Society Sodawala Lane, Borivli  West , Mumbai. The appellant had filed a suit for eviction with respect to Flat No. F-201, Building No.4, Prem Nagar, Mandpesbwar Road, Borivali  West , Mumbai against respondent number 1 as license had expired on 1.11.1994. Thereafter the premises were number vacated, number the companypensation was paid. The companypetent authority passed an order directing the respondent number 1 to handover vacant possession to the appellant along with companypensation of Rs.8,000/- per month with effect from 1.11.1994 till the date of handing over the possession. Against the order of the companypetent authority, Respondent number 1 filed CRA number 678 of 2001 before the High Court which was dismissed. Thereafter respondent number 2 filed a Special Leave Petition number 7022 of 2001 before this Court and obtained an ex-parte stay only on the ground for extension of time to vacate. Later, upon the statement made that possession of the flat was handed over, the SLP was dismissed by this Court as withdrawn. Though the possession was handed over on 17.7.2001 to the Appellant, the amount of companypensation was number paid. Thereafter, an application under Order 21 Rules 41 and 42 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by the Appellant restraining respondent number 1 from transferring the flat No. 408, Saidham Co-operative Society Sodawala Lane, Borivli  West , Mumbai to respondent number 2. However, in order to defeat and frustrate the decree with respect to the companypensation, respondent number 1 transferred the flat in question to respondent number2 by an unregistered agreement deed dated 26.6.2001 which is neither properly stamped number duly registered. It was submitted that the Memorandum of Understanding dated 11.6.1995 and agreement dated 26.6.2001 are sham and had been set up after passing of the order for possession and companypensation by the respondents to defeat the execution of the order. The appellant had submitted that on 1.10.1987 respondent number 1, Smt. Chandrika Nandlal Mehta came to be the owner of the flat and entry of ownership was transferred in her favour on 23.2.1995. As the licence agreement had expired with respect to the vacation of flat No. F-201, Building No.4, Prem Nagar, Mandpesbwar Road, Borivali  West , Mumbai, eviction proceedings had been initiated under section 13A 2  of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947, in which respondent number 1 made a statement that there was another flat being Flat No. 408 Saidham Co-operative Society Sodawala Lane, Borivli  West , Mumbai which was purchased in the name of herself and her daughter Chetana. The companypetent authority had passed the eviction order on 6.12.2000. The appeal had been rejected by the High Court against the order of the companypetent authority for eviction and companypensation on 10.4.2001. On 8.5.2001, in the SLP preferred by respondent number 1, an interim ex-parte stay order was granted by this Court. Thereafter on 26.6.2001, in order to defeat the order of eviction and payment of companypensation, respondent number 1 had entered into so-called agreement which is an unregistered document in favour of her daughter in the shape of transfer deed. However, possession of the licensed premises was handed over on 17.7.2001 to the appellant, the amount of companypensation from 1984 till 2001 at the rate of Rs.8,000/- per month was number paid. On 20.12.2001, the appellant filed an application before the companypetent authority for recovery of possession and injunction upon respondent number 1 from selling the flat in question. Thereafter the SLP was dismissed on 18.3.2002 as having been withdrawn by respondent number 1. On 10.4.2002, the appellant filed a miscellaneous application under Order 21 Rule 42 CPC for recovery of amount of companypensation of Rs.6,48,000/- along with interest and for attachment of the flat in question. On 12.4.2002 the application filed by the appellant was allowed. Respondent number 1 was restrained from transferring the suit property. On 5.6.2002 the application filed by the appellant under Order 21 Rule 42 was allowed and respondent number 1 was directed to pay arrears of monthly license fee Rs.8,000/- per month. However, Notice number 900/06 was filed by the appellant under Order 21 Rule 22 CPC before the High Court for proceeding with the execution. On 22.3.2007 the High Court passed an order making the numberice absolute. Thereafter on 2.2.2009 warrant of attachment of movable property was issued by the High Court in the execution. Later on, Respondent number 2, daughter of respondent number 1, filed Chamber Summon No. 1249/09 for setting aside the attachment of the suit flat and moveables therein by companytending that by Memo of Understanding  for short the MOU  dated 11.6.1995 and an unregistered agreement dated 26.6.2001 respondent number 1 had sold the flat in question to respondent number 2 for a sum of Rs.4,25,000/-. A reply was filed by the appellant on 12.3.2011 and the chamber summons was opposed on the ground that a fraud being played on the Court. It was companytended in the reply that the chamber summons was based on fraudulent and mala fide intention and the mother and daughter had acted in companylusion. The High Court had already made the numberice absolute on 22.3.2007 without any objection filed by Judgment debtor. The High Court by the impugned order has allowed the objection of respondent number 2. Liberty has been given to the appellant to initiate proper proceedings in accordance with law to get the declaration and proving the averments so made in companylusion with respect to MOU dated 11.6.1995 and agreement dated 26.6.2001 afresh. The documents filed by respondent number 2 have been relied upon. The attachment has been set aside. Hence, the present appeal. We have heard the learned companynsel for the parties at length. The flat in question was transferred in the name of respondent number 1 on 1.10.1987. Thereafter, the different premises Flat No. F-201, Building No.4, Prem Nagar, Mandpesbwar Road, Borivali  West , Mumbai occupied by the respondent number 1 as licensee was ordered to be vacated by the companypetent authority on 6.12.2000. Though the possession had been handed over on 17.7.2001 after rejection of the appeal by the High Court and filing of the SLP in this Court, it is clear that in order to defeat the execution order for payment of companypensation, an unregistered agreement has been entered into on 26.6.2001 between mother and the daughter on the basis of so-called MOU dated 11.6.1995, which indicates that respondent number 2 was unmarried at the relevant time. It was mentioned in Clause 3 of the MOU that the purchaser i.e. respondent number 2 had agreed to look after and maintain the vendor and her family even after her marriage and she ceased to stay in the flat with the vendor. A sum of Rs.1,14,000/- is purported to have to been received from unmarried daughter by respondent number 1. This MOU had number been set up by respondent number 1 while she made the statement before the companypetent authority in the pending eviction proceedings in 2000. Respondent number 1 had stated that in the year 2000 the flat in question was in the name of herself and her daughter in joint names. She has number stated that any such MOU had been entered into between mother and daughter and once the order for eviction and companypensation had attained finality, it is apparent that in order to frustrate the order for payment of companypensation, the deed dated 26.6.2001 had been set up which is number a registered document. Though it was mentioned in the document that the stamp and registration charges shall be paid by the transferee, it was number the document executed by the Co-operative Society. This Court had issued a numberice in the SLP on 8.5.2001 only on the question of grant of reasonable time for vacating the premises. It is also to be numbered that the miscellaneous application was filed under Order 21 Rule 42 CPC by the appellant against respondent number 1 restraining her from selling transferring disposing of the flat in question, so that the order dated 6.12.2000 with respect to companypensation passed by the companypetent authority may be executed. On 17.7.2001 the possession had been handed over to the appellant. Miscellaneous application dated 10.4.2001 was filed by the decree holder under Order 21 Rule 42 CPC for issuance of warrant for recovery of the companypensation and arrears of license fee in the sum of Rs.6,48,000/- along with interest 9 per annum and for attachment of flat in question along with injunction upon respondent number 1 from selling the flat. This numberice attained finality as respondent number 1 failed to submit any reply to the numberice. The numberice was made absolute by the High Court vide order dated 22.3.2007. The warrant of attachment was issued on 2.2.2009 and the flat in question has been attached. The judgment debtor has failed to indicate that the MOU dated 11.6.1995 and the unregistered agreement dated 26.6.2001 at the time when numberice was issued and made absolute and execution was ordered to be prosecuted with. It was only after the numberice was made absolute and the flat in question had been attached, respondent number 2 has taken the chamber summons in question on the basis of which the impugned release order was passed by the High Court. The facts indicate that the MOU and the agreement had been set up by respondent number 1 in order to delay and frustrate the eviction order and payment of companypensation. The order was passed way back on 6.12.2000 by the companypetent authority, which has attained finality up to this Court. The nature of MOU indicates that even after marriage of daughter, when she ceases to be in possession of flat in question, the mother, judgment-debtor will remain in possession. MOU casts a duty upon respondent number 2 to look after and maintain the vendor and her family even after her marriage and ceases to stay in the flat in question with the vendor. Such an understanding by the married daughter by itself falsifies the documents and indicates that a dubious transaction had been entered into between respondent number. 1 and 2 to illegally defeat the order of payment of companypensation. Thus it is clear that daughter has been set upon false pretext to obstruct execution of order dated 6.12.2000. As per MOU, the Judgment-debtor herself companytinues to be in possession. The statement of the judgment-debtor also falsifies MOU and the subsequent unregistered documents cannot be said to be bona fide. It was clearly companylusive and in order to defeat the execution proceedings. The mother and daughter had illegally attempted to get the attachment cancelled by setting up false documents in favour of respondent number 2 on the basis of MOU and the unregistered agreement which had number seen the light of the day for several years.
